short: The conditions in which people are born, grow, live, work and age — and their access to power, money and resources.
definition: WHO defines the social determinants of health as the conditions in which people are born, grow, live, work and age, and people's access to power, money and resources [56]. Healthy People 2030 adds learning, playing and worshipping, and groups them into five domains [57].

short: The context and stratifying mechanisms — income, education, occupation, class, gender, race/ethnicity — that set people's social position.
definition: In the WHO conceptual framework, structural determinants are the socioeconomic and political context, the mechanisms that stratify society, and the resulting socioeconomic position of individuals; they act through intermediary determinants [2].

short: Material and psychosocial circumstances, behaviours and biology, and the health system — the routes structural determinants act through.
definition: The WHO conceptual framework names four groups of intermediary determinants: material circumstances, psychosocial circumstances, behavioural and biological factors, and the health system itself [2].

short: Health improves step by step with social position, not just between the poorest and everyone else.
definition: In US tax and death records, higher income was associated with greater longevity throughout the income distribution, not only at the bottom [11].

short: A social condition, such as income or education, that keeps shaping health even as the specific risk factors change.
definition: Socioeconomic factors such as income, wealth and education have been described as fundamental causes of a wide range of health outcomes [3].

short: WHO's International Classification of Diseases, 11th revision; its Chapter 24 codes social circumstances (QD50–QE9Z).
definition: ICD-11 for Mortality and Morbidity Statistics is WHO's classification. Its Chapter 24 section 'Factors influencing health status' has blocks QD50–QE9Z for problems associated with finances, housing and environment, employment, education, the social environment, justice, relationships, loss, family, trauma and upbringing [59].

short: The ICD-10-CM categories Z55–Z65 used in the US to record social determinants in health records.
definition: In ICD-10-CM, categories Z55–Z65 record problems related to education, employment, occupational exposure, physical environment, housing and economic circumstances, social environment, upbringing, primary support group and psychosocial circumstances [58].

short: A map of variables joined by signed arrows (+ or −) that shows the feedback loops in a system.
definition: A diagram of variables joined by arrows marked + or −. System dynamics uses such feedback maps to study public-health problems [51].

short: + if the effect moves in the same direction as the cause (all else equal); − if it moves the opposite way.
definition: In this app: + means the effect moves the same way as the cause, all else equal; − means the opposite way.

short: A loop with an even number of − links: a change travels round and comes back amplified.
definition: In this app: a loop whose link signs multiply to + (an even number of − links), so a change returns amplified.

short: A loop with an odd number of − links: a change travels round and comes back opposed.
definition: In this app: a loop whose link signs multiply to − (an odd number of − links), so a change returns opposed.

short: A path that returns to its start without visiting any node twice — what the app lists as a loop.
definition: An elementary circuit of a directed graph is a closed path with no repeated vertex; Johnson's algorithm finds all of them in time proportional to the graph's size times the number of circuits [49].

short: A group of nodes that all reach each other through arrows — the parts of a map that sit inside shared feedback.
definition: Graph partitions that contain all of a model's feedback loops can be found and decomposed with graph theory, giving a granular view of feedback complexity [50].

short: Your judgement of how strongly one circumstance pushes another, from −1 to +1 — not a measured effect size.
definition: In this app: your judgement of a link's strength, from −1 to +1, matching its polarity. Not a measured effect size.

short: A node that network measures flag as central — a prompt for discussion, not proof of where to act.
definition: Network-analytic measures applied to a causal loop diagram can flag central variables as candidate leverage points [52].

short: Abuse, neglect and household dysfunction in childhood — linked to adult health and to adult education, work and income.
definition: Adverse childhood experiences include childhood abuse and household dysfunction [19]. People with four or more have higher risks across many health outcomes [34], and higher ACE scores are associated with lower education, unemployment and poverty in adulthood [35].

short: Prolonged, unbuffered stress in early childhood that can leave lasting effects on development and health.
definition: An ecobiodevelopmental framework describes how early adversity and toxic stress can leave a lasting signature on the genetic predispositions that affect emerging brain architecture and long-term health [36].

short: The ability to find, understand and use health information.
definition: Low health literacy is consistently associated with more hospitalisations, more emergency care, lower receipt of screening and vaccination, and poorer ability to demonstrate taking medications appropriately [32].

short: The idea that social support protects people from the harm of stressful events.
definition: The buffering model holds that social support protects people from the adverse effects of stressful events; evidence fits it when support is measured as perceived availability of help, and a main effect when measured as network integration [44].

short: Having few social contacts (objective) or feeling alone (subjective); both are linked to earlier death.
definition: Social isolation, loneliness and living alone are each associated with increased mortality, with effects comparable to well-established risk factors [38].

short: Involuntary removal from a home — linked to hardship, depression and later job loss.
definition: Eviction is followed by more material hardship, depression and parenting stress among low-income mothers [22], and forced moves are followed by a higher likelihood of being laid off [23].
